paragraphs: No new independent shock this week - this is the same rates/inflation throughline from the Sept 16 FOMC continuing to grind, with a notable reversal right at the end. The 10-year Treasury yield kept climbing through Tuesday Sept 29, touching roughly 5.29% intraday (highest since 2007), while the 30-year pushed above 5.6% - its highest since June 2002 - as sticky inflation expectations (the University of Michigan's year-ahead inflation gauge jumped to 4.6% in September from 4.0% in August, the highest since June), heavy Treasury/corporate bond issuance, and a growing federal debt load (near $40 trillion) kept pressure on the long end. That pressure eased abruptly on Wednesday Sept 30 when the PCE inflation print landed below expectations and Fed officials' commentary pulled market-implied odds of an October hike down to under 40% (from the 66-74% priced in as of the Sept 23 pull) - the Nasdaq rallied to close out Q3 on the news.

Credit markets diverged from equities over the same stretch: the ICE BofA High Yield OAS widened roughly 46bps (from about 2.66% on Sept 21 to 3.12% by Sept 30), a five-month high, as a record $38.5B of September high-yield issuance - including SoftBank's $10B bond and Paramount Skydance's $44.4B financing package - tested investors' capacity to absorb new supply even as equities sat near highs; analysts flagged the resulting credit-equity divergence as a risk signal worth watching, not yet a stress event (IG spreads barely moved, and the VIX term structure stayed in calm contango). None of this tripped this dashboard's day-move materiality thresholds the way the last two pulls' sharp single/two-day swings did: over the five trading days through Oct 1 the S&P 500, Nasdaq, and Dow were all roughly flat-to-down low-single-digits (-0.5%, -0.3%, -0.8% respectively) and the Russell 2000 -1.0% - a genuinely quieter week, not the story disappearing.

Separately on data quality: this dashboard's free FRED oil-price source (DCOILWTICO) printed an implausible run this stretch ($85.23 on Sept 25, $99.37 on Sept 28, $96.16 on Sept 29) that independent sources (Investing.com, Robinhood's WTI prediction-market data) don't corroborate - real WTI traded in a comparatively narrower ~$89-94 band across the same days. Real oil-market volatility was genuinely elevated (the Brent-WTI spread blew out to ~$12.83, its widest since May, as Brent drew a geopolitical premium from stalled Hormuz reopening talks while WTI weakened on US diesel-export-ban talk and rising Saudi/UAE exports), but FRED's specific day-to-day dollar swings over Sept 25-29 look like a data-quality issue rather than a real move of that size - logged in WISHLIST.md, and this pull's oil-move flag narrative cites the real, independently-reported ~3.5-3.8% WTI decline on Sept 29 rather than FRED's own likely-wrong dollar levels.

Markets gave back a chunk of last week's rally over these two sessions, and the story is a direct continuation/intensification of the rates-and-inflation throughline running since the Sept 16 FOMC hike, not a new independent shock.

Tuesday Sept 22 was mixed - the Nasdaq notched a second straight record close (+0.4%) as Meta's Muse-driven chip-sector optimism carried over and oil initially fell ~3% on an Iranian signal it would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if U.S. military pressure eased, while the Dow slipped 0.3% and Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin warned 'supply shocks aren't proving short-lived' (a hawkish signal) and oil pared its drop back after President Trump told the UN a U.S.-Iran deal wouldn't come before the November midterms.

Wednesday Sept 23 reversed hard across the board: the 10-year Treasury yield surged to roughly 5.11%-5.14% - the highest since July 2007 - after Fed Governor Michael Barr said 'further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion,' and a much-hotter-than-expected S&P Global composite PMI (58.4 vs. 55.3 forecast) reinforced the inflation picture, pushing market-implied odds of an October hike to roughly 66-74%. All three major indices fell Wednesday (Dow -0.7%, S&P 500 -0.8%, Nasdaq -1.1%), with the Russell 2000 leading declines (-1.77% Wednesday alone) on its usual higher rate sensitivity, and breadth was lopsided across this dashboard's filtered universe (495 advancers vs. 799 decliners). No single new dominant catalyst beyond the yield/Fed-hawkishness combination - this reads as profit-taking and rate repricing after last week's rally, not a fresh shock requiring a rewrite of the underlying framing below.

Data note: Tuesday Sept 22 is missing entirely from the free Yahoo history endpoint this dashboard's index and universe data comes from, both for the headline indices and the ~1,300-name equity universe; this was confirmed via search to be a genuine data gap, not a market holiday - Sept 22, 2026 was an ordinary Tuesday trading session per multiple outlets' live market coverage, so figures described as a single 'day move' below actually span two real sessions, Tue Sept 22 and Wed Sept 23, compressed together by the gap.

newly_flagged.narrative: UPDATE (this pull, 2026-10-01): This flag trips on FRED's own -3.2% day-change figure (from an implausible $99.37 print on Sept 28 to $96.16 on Sept 29 - see this pull's synthesis and WISHLIST.md for why those specific FRED dollar levels look like a data-quality issue), but the direction and rough magnitude are genuinely real: independent sources put WTI's actual Sept 29 close around $89.38-90.54, down roughly 3.5-3.8% on the day from a comparatively stable ~$92-93 the prior several sessions. The real driver was a combination of a much wider Brent-WTI spread (blown out to ~$12.83, its widest since May) and broad bearish fundamentals: Brent held a geopolitical premium (above $103-107) as U.S. President Trump rejected Iran's conditional offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days on Sept 26, while WTI specifically weakened on US diesel-export-ban talk, higher freight costs, rising Saudi/UAE exports (Gulf crude exports hit their highest level since February, ~12.8M bbl/day), and sharply cut 2026 demand forecasts from OPEC and the IEA alongside a large US inventory build - a bearish-fundamentals move for the US benchmark specifically, not a resolution of the still-live Middle East supply risk that keeps Brent elevated. Prior framing: UPDATE (this pull, 2026-09-17): WTI has kept climbing since last pull, trading near $102-104/bbl into and through the Sept 16 FOMC decision (Brent briefly above $108 before easing) as Iran-backed Houthi militants advance toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and intensify attacks on Saudi targets and shipping routes, reportedly prompting Saudi Aramco to delay some European deliveries. The Fed's own statement cited Middle East tension as a factor in its decision, directly linking this flag to the yield-move flag above. Prior framing: WTI crude's jump reflects Middle East supply fears after Iran's attacks on commercial and U.S. Navy vessels, which the Iranian Foreign Ministry has framed as retaliatory. Brent has held above $90/bbl. Higher oil adds to the inflation picture the Fed is already responding to, reinforcing (not just coinciding with) this week's yield move.

Wednesday Sept 23 did the rest of the damage (-0.7%) as the 10-year Treasury yield jumped to roughly 5.11%-5.14% (highest since July 2007) after Fed Governor Michael Barr said 'further policy adjustments are likely to be needed,' and a hotter-than-expected S&P Global composite PMI (58.4 vs. 55.3 forecast) reinforced inflation concerns, pushing October-hike odds to ~66-74%. Prior framing: UPDATE (this pull, 2026-09-17): This flag now trips on the day-move threshold rather than the 5-day one, because the FOMC's Sept 16 hike hit in a single session: the Fed hiked 25bp as anticipated, and the Dow fell 631pts (-1.21%) to 51,461.90 on the day — banks led the damage (KBE -2.6%, worst day since February) on fears the hiking cycle continues into 2027. Prior framing: broad-market and cyclical names have lagged over the past week as rising Treasury yields and oil prices weigh on rate-sensitive and industrial stocks more than mega-cap tech. A hot core CPI print (+0.3% m/m vs +0.2% forecast) raised the odds of a Fed hike at the Sept 15-16 FOMC meeting from ~70% to ~90%, and Iran's attacks on commercial/naval vessels in the Middle East have pushed oil higher, adding an inflation and cost headwind for industrials and consumer names that make up a larger share of the Dow than the Nasdaq.
